findings: The parent creates one private scratch directory and records its filesystem identity before spawning each worker. The spawn entry redirects tempfile and TMPDIR/TEMP/TMP only in that child, confining both GPT-2 and Qwen verified copies without changing public consumer APIs, snapshot bytes or persistent authority.

Successful completion, startup failure, killed child, timeout and malformed worker transport all reach cleanup. Child termination must be confirmed by process liveness and exit status before reclamation. No global temporary-directory search or unrelated path deletion is introduced.

Cleanup verifies root directory type/device/inode, handles sealed readonly artifacts, rejects changed ownership, and refuses symlink escapes. Comparing resolved child paths to a resolved admitted root also supports system temporary parents that are themselves symlink aliases.

Cleanup failure or unconfirmed death prevents a successful outcome and becomes runner_error. Observed event bodies and known token subtotals remain retained; unknown completion remains conservative. Scratch is retained when deletion cannot safely be attempted.

Tests exercise actual spawned GPT-2 and Qwen private-copy admission followed by SIGKILL, timeout and ordinary completion; they verify death before deletion, unchanged parent temp settings, source bytes and authority/evidence/sibling sentinels.

Additional controls cover process-start failure, explicit PermissionError recovery, external symlink targets, changed root ownership, cleanup refusal and uncertain child death. No tiny-fixture test claims pretrained task quality.
limitations: Whole-parent death can still leave scratch and remains a separately documented recovery obligation.
The cleanup protocol assumes the surviving supervisor controls its worker; it is not a general sandbox against arbitrary same-user concurrent filesystem attackers.
